subtype: Approach: writing a small note if talking feels too hard [Action]
passage: Class teacher's note, Thursday. During free reading I saw Pema, the quietest girl in the row, take out a torn page and write something slowly, crossing out two lines. After two days of not speaking to her friend Vikas, Pema had shouted at recess on Tuesday and seemed too embarrassed to say anything. Pema folded the page small and slipped it into Vikas's desk, then went back to a book without turning a page. Vikas found it after the bell and read it twice: "I'm sorry I yelled. Want to be friends again?" By afternoon Vikas had left a reply on Pema's desk. I did not step in. Both seem lighter.

qa.q: Where did Pema put the folded page?
qa.a: Pema slipped it into Vikas's desk.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling while writing and slipping the note away?
qa.a: Pema was probably shy and embarrassed, shown by writing slowly, crossing out lines and pretending to read afterwards.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Pema use if a note does not get an answer, and why?
qa.a: Pema could ask the teacher to help the two of them talk, or wait for a calm moment to speak in person. A helper can make a hard conversation easier.

qa.q: How does Vikas experience the note?
qa.a: Vikas read it twice and left a reply, so the note gave Vikas time to take in the apology and answer without pressure.

grounding: A shy girl who finds speaking hard writes a short note asking to be friends, and the note gives the friend time to feel and reply.

subtype: Approach: writing a small note if talking feels too hard [Action]
passage:
Thursday night
Yesterday I shouted at Zubin in the art room because he spilled water on my painting. I've felt sick in my stomach about it ever since. Today I tried three times to go and say sorry, but my mouth closed every time. I'm like that; the other girls say I'm too quiet, and my voice just disappears. So in maths I tore a page from the back of my notebook and wrote: 'Zubin, I'm sorry I yelled. It was only paint. Friends again? Hansa.' I folded it small and slipped it into his desk before lunch. After lunch there was a paper boat on my desk. Inside: 'Yes. Sorry about the water 🙂'

qa.q: What did Hansa find on her desk after lunch?
qa.a: A paper boat, with 'Yes. Sorry about the water' inside.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel about shouting at Zubin?
qa.a: Hansa felt guilty and anxious about it, sick in the stomach ever since.

qa.q: Why was a note a good choice for Hansa?
qa.a: Her voice disappears when she's nervous, so writing let her say sorry clearly and gave Zubin time to reply.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt finding the note?
qa.a: Zubin seemed relieved and ready to make up, replying 'Yes' and saying sorry for the water too.

grounding: Shows a shy girl who cannot say sorry aloud writing a short note and putting it in her friend's desk, giving the friend time to reply.

subtype: Approach: writing a small note if talking feels too hard [Action]
passage: At the village school Tanuja hardly spoke above a whisper, except on Monday, when she had shouted at Nirmala for stepping on her skipping rope. Everyone had turned to look. Now, two days later, Tanuja couldn't find her voice at all. After the prayer bell she tore the corner off her notebook and wrote slowly: 'I am sorry for shouting. Will you skip with me again?' She folded it into a tiny square and pushed it into Nirmala's desk while the others were filling water. Nirmala found it during the Hindi lesson, read it twice, and didn't look up. Tanuja's heart thumped. At the end of school, Nirmala was waiting by the gate, holding the rope.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja's heart thump during the Hindi lesson?
qa.a: She felt nervous and anxious, not knowing how Nirmala would react, because Nirmala didn't look up.

qa.q: What made the note work well here?
qa.a: It let shy Tanuja say sorry without speaking, and gave Nirmala time to read it twice and decide how to answer.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt reading the note twice?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt touched and took time to think, then answered by waiting at the gate with the rope.

grounding: Illustrates a shy girl writing a sorry note and slipping it into her friend's desk, which gives the friend time to feel and respond.
